review:
Induction, developed and published by Bryan Gale, is a cerebral puzzle game that builds its entire identity around the manipulation of time, transforming a simple concept into something surprisingly intricate. At a glance, it appears minimal—guiding a small cube across floating platforms toward a goal—but this simplicity quickly gives way to a system that challenges players to think across multiple timelines at once. It is less about movement and more about understanding how actions ripple through time, creating a puzzle structure that feels both elegant and demanding.

The central mechanic allows players to rewind their actions and create “echoes” of previous movements. These echoes replay exactly what the player did in the past, effectively turning earlier decisions into tools that can interact with the present. This creates a layered form of problem-solving where players must coordinate multiple versions of themselves, ensuring that each iteration contributes to a larger solution. What begins as a straightforward concept evolves into increasingly complex scenarios, where timing, positioning, and foresight all intersect.

As the game progresses, it expands on this idea without ever abandoning its core. New elements are introduced gradually, adding depth without overwhelming the player immediately. However, the difficulty ramps up significantly, requiring players to think several steps ahead and consider how each action will be repeated and combined. The puzzles often demand a precise understanding of cause and effect, and solutions can feel elusive until the underlying logic becomes clear. This progression creates a strong sense of intellectual challenge, rewarding persistence and careful reasoning.

One of the defining aspects of Induction is its approach to teaching. The game provides minimal direct instruction, instead relying on players to learn through experimentation. While this design fosters a sense of discovery, it can also lead to moments of confusion, particularly when new mechanics are introduced without clear explanation. The lack of guidance is a deliberate choice, encouraging players to engage more deeply with the systems, but it may not appeal to those who prefer more structured learning.

The visual presentation reflects the game’s focus on clarity and abstraction. Environments are composed of simple geometric shapes and soft colors, creating a clean and uncluttered space that keeps attention on the puzzles. This minimalism ensures that even complex scenarios remain readable, which is essential given the layered nature of the gameplay. The accompanying soundtrack is subtle and ambient, providing a calm backdrop that contrasts with the mental intensity of solving the puzzles.

Despite its strengths, the game’s design also introduces some limitations. The difficulty can become quite steep, especially in later stages, where puzzles require a high level of precision and understanding. This can lead to frustration, particularly when progress stalls and the solution is not immediately apparent. Additionally, the abstract presentation and lack of narrative context may make it harder for some players to stay engaged over longer sessions.

Replayability is also limited by the nature of the puzzles. Once a solution has been discovered, the challenge largely disappears, as the experience is rooted in first-time problem-solving rather than variation. While the game offers a substantial number of levels, its long-term appeal depends heavily on the player’s enjoyment of its core mechanic.

Even with these challenges, Induction succeeds in delivering a unique and thoughtfully designed puzzle experience. It explores its central idea with depth and consistency, creating a series of challenges that feel both cohesive and rewarding. The interplay between past and present actions gives the game a distinctive identity, setting it apart from more conventional puzzle titles.

In the end, Induction is a demanding but highly satisfying game that rewards patience and analytical thinking. It may not be accessible to everyone, but for those willing to engage with its systems, it offers a memorable and intellectually stimulating journey through time-based problem-solving.

Induction is a puzzle game with the concept of using time travel to beat the levels.  

For the achievement hunter, it is a very straight forward completion: simply beat all of the levels. Now, there are no secret levels, collectibles or speedrunning involved. But to make things easier there are two things that I would recommend. Besides the more obvious alternative to use a guide with the solutions, I would recommend to activate the grid so that you actually see where exactly you are and where you have to go. The average completion time for Induction is around 8-9 hours, but you will do it faster if you use a guide from the start. 

Induction has a very interesting concept with it's time travel mechanic, making the levels feel more clever and about timing than difficulty. I believe that a average puzzle enjoyer can solve most of the puzzles without using a guide once you get a understanding of how the mechanic works. I would recommend the game for both casual puzzle players and achievement hunters, but given the game's length and content, I can't recommend it at full price (fortunately it has had discounts of up to -75%!).

One of the puzzle greats. I'm talking Stephen's Sausage Roll, Snakebird, Baba Is You, Magicube, etc. You liked those games? You'll love this.

Of all of those puzzle games, I think Induction takes the cake for being the hardest to make sense of what you're doing, at least while mechanics are still being introduced and haven't had time to settle. It's like that scene from Tenet: don't try to think too hard about it, just [i]feel[/i] it. Indeed, by the end of the game you'll have developed a sort of second-nature to how go about solving these time conundrums. When the developer said it will rewire how you think about cause and effect - they weren't joking.

Pair that with the fact that mechanics are rarely tutorialized beyond dropping you in a room and giving you a button prompt, part of the puzzle of Induction often becomes figuring out what [i]exactly[/i] it is that that new mechanic you just learned a few levels ago [i]actually does at a conceptual level[/i] so you can exploit it to its fullest.

Induction has no wasted space - almost to a fault, however. While every single puzzle is top notch, I feel like there easily could have been several more late-game puzzles added to it to extend the game's length. The difficulty spike between the last and second to last puzzles seems strong evidence of this, especially because that last level makes use of essentially two new mechanics, each of which could have easily generated more puzzles on their own. [spoiler]That being the collectible that lets you shift time 5 times instead of the previous 3, and also the idea of standing on one of your clone's head, which as far as I recall was never a necessary part of a puzzle solution before that point, despite being something you could do from the beginning.[/spoiler]

The isometric art style as well as the fact that the buttons do not show you what paths they will activate before you interact with them do make it a little difficult to discern exactly how certain puzzles are rigged up, but this is rarely that big of an issue. Just know that a fairly small amount of your time will be spent figuring out how certain levels are rigged up. In my opinion, I actually think this aspect works to the game's benefit, because it gives you sort of a meta-level goal when you first open a level that helps prevent you from getting overwhelmed. You don't need to figure out how to get to the exit just yet, you just need to figure out how to get to that button so you can figure out what it does. And in figuring out how to get to that button, you're already on your way to solving the entire puzzle. In some puzzles, it sort of fragments the level into multiple micro puzzles that you can solve that all accumulate into the larger puzzle. This is how I felt especially of the last puzzle, where a key bit of information on how the puzzle was even possible was not immediately accessible without having solved half the puzzle already.

One minor gripe I have with the game is that (since it is real-time and not turn-based) you will sometimes just have to press a button down to pass time while your clones are doing actions and wait for "your turn" to do something. For the first 3/4 of the game, this is rarely an issue as the amount of time you are usually waiting for is very small. But with some puzzles (and especially that last puzzle) you could be sitting there holding a button down for a dozen seconds or more. This time accumulates pretty quick when you're bound to get certain things wrong on your first attempt and then have to undo and retry, forcing you to hold that button and wait for a dozen more seconds, and then a dozen more. It rarely affected my enjoyment of the game; that last puzzle is still one of my favorites. And again, it's only really noticeable on some of the later puzzles, and I'm not exactly sure if there was a better way this could have been implemented, as time is such a core part of how these puzzles are rigged up.

All in all, if you're up for a challenge, Induction is a great brain-buster that is worth your time and every penny.

在其它艺术形式如小说，电影中，创作一个时间穿越类题材，且是宿命论的作品是可行的。这是因为无论小说也好，电影也罢，它们都在讲故事，而故事中的主角是没有自由意志的，作者想让它们干嘛就干嘛。但把这任务放到在游戏中，就出问题了。这其实也体现出游戏这一艺术形式与其它艺术形式的本质区别——参与者（游戏里就是玩家，小说和电影里分别是读者与观众）具备自由意志，能够左右作品故事情节和内容的发展。
Induction中，玩家按空格键可以穿越回过去，而游戏通关条件便是玩家抵达终点并且过去的自己抵达穿越点。前面说了，做一个祖父悖论宿命论的游戏会出问题，而Induction的“问题”便是玩家在穿越前，无法看到未来穿越到现在的自己。这也间接导致一些原本能靠时间穿越能力解决的谜题无法实现。举个简单的例子，玩家被一个只能从后面打开的门挡住，而他拥有时间穿越的能力，本来他完全可以靠未来穿越回现在的自己在门后出现，打开门并让现在的他能够达到门后再原地穿越，从而实现闭环。但在Induction则不行，因为玩家无法“召唤”未来的自己。
Induction其实是一个祖父悖论，半宿命论，半平行宇宙论的游戏。玩家穿越到的其实是另一个平行宇宙，只是这个宇宙中的主角会干玩家之前做过的同样的事情。在此基础上作者还给游戏添加了一个“宿命论”的通关条件，那便是这个宇宙的主角最后的穿越点必须与上一个平行宇宙的玩家一致。
关于“线条圈”这一元素的机制，其实就是在解决玩家无法“召唤”未来的自己的问题。线条圈可以让来自上一个平行宇宙的主角消失，将控制权给予这个宇宙的主角并令其不必复刻上一个主角的行迹，唯一的改变便是保留了上一个主角对这个世界产生的影响——如将一个箱子推到一个位置上，并且开始控制这个世界的主角的时间并非这个世界的最初时间。所以玩家便可以默认未来穿越回过去的自己能够达成这个被保留的影响，从而打开“只能从后面打开的门”。
游戏的谜题设计，音乐和视觉效果体验下来都不错，推荐。

[h1] Induction; un agréable vent de fraîcheur [/h1]

Induction. Premièrement, définissons le mot. Comme je ne suis pas un dictionnaire, j'emprunte la définition que me fournit Google:"Transmission d'énergie électrique ou magnétique par l'intermédiaire d'un aimant ou d'un courant". Pour ce qui est du jeu dont on parle aujourd'hui, concentrons-nous sur la partie qui mentionne "transmission d'énergie". Vous comprendrez un peu plus loin si vous continuez à lire.

[b] La mécanique principale du jeu [/b]

Induction n'a pas de tutoriel en bonne et due forme. Au début, on est un peu mêlés, mais rapidement, nous comprenons ce qu'il faut faire. Ça pourra paraître compliqué, mais c'est assez simple. Commençons par la base. Nous sommes un cube et dans chaque tableau, notre but est d'aller au point d'arrivée. Classique. Mais la première chose qui nous frappe est que le premier tableau est "impossible" à première vue. Bon, quoi faire? La twist est qu'en appuyant sur la barre d'espace de votre clavier, vous déclencherez un nouveau cube allié et vous réalisez ensuite que votre premier cube est là pour vous aider, mais que vous ne le contrôlez pas puisqu'il ne fera que les mouvements que vous avez fait dans le passé, comme si ces mouvements avaient été enregistrées. Vous enregistrez les mouvements du cube 1, vous déclenchez un cube 2, ce qui remettra les pendules à 0 et pendant que vous bougerez votre cube 2, votre cube 1 fera le trajet que vous lui avez fait faire.

Il faut donc calculer son temps correctement. Si par exemple j'ai besoin que bloc 1 pousse bloc 2 à un moment précis, je devrai faire en sorte d'anticiper le chemin que je prendrai avec bloc 2 et calculer le temps que cela devrait me prendre. Ou encore, pour le phraser autrement, lorsque vous activez bloc 2, vous cohabitez avec bloc 1 qui fera exactement les mouvements que vous avez fait comme s'ils avaient été enregistrés.

Alors voilà, vous bougez votre cube 1 en sachant que tous vos mouvements sont enregistrés et que lorsque vous activez le cube 2, le cube 1 refera votre chemin. Vous devrez donc avec votre cube 1 faire le trajet nécessaire, non pas pour apporter votre cube à destination, mais pour aider votre futur cube 2 à arriver à sa destination.

[b] Une agréable surprise [/b]

Je ne sais pas pour vous, mais je trouve le procédé très intéressant. Je ne dis pas que c'est du jamais vu (n'hésitez pas à commenter si jamais vous connaissez d'autres jeux avec cette mécanique ou une mécanique similaire), mais c'est la première fois que je joue à un jeu de puzzle qui la propose et j'avoue être séduit.

Bon, mon temps de jeu est modeste au moment d'écrire cette évaluation, mais je voulais partager mes impressions à froid comme ça puisque j'ai été emballé par l'originalité d'Induction.

[b] Appréciations personnelles [/b]

L'esthétique est froide et aurait pu être plus travaillée, mais pour le prix, je n'ai pas à me plaindre. Vous pourrez peut-être vous le procurer à bon prix dans un bundle Steam. Selon mon évaluation aucunement scientifique, j'imagine que vous en aurez pour 18 heures environ pour compléter tous les tableaux, peut-être plus si vous êtes un joueur lent comme moi. J'ai dit plus haut que l'esthétique du jeu n'était pas des plus travaillée, mais tout est quand même très clair et visuellement facile à comprendre.

L'autre exploit d'Induction est que son gameplay est aussi très plaisant. Parce que ce n'est pas tout de proposer un gameplay original, encore faut-il qu'il soit plaisant. J'ai joué un peu plus de 30 minutes seulement et déjà, de nouvelles mécaniques font leur apparition. Mais le noyau central reste les 2 cubes dans 2 espace-temps si je peux me permettre cette expression.

[b] Conclusion [/b]

Si vous aimez les jeux de puzzle, que vous aimiez ou non Induction après y avoir joué, je crois que vous serez content de l'avoir essayé. C'est selon moi une addition essentielle à la bibliothèque de tous les amateurs de jeux de puzzle.

Bravo au développeur pour son originalité.

I will say that I definitely like the basic idea of Induction, but the execution left me confused and frustrated. The goal is to get your cube to the end of the level. You can create a clone that mimics your actions you took up until that point, which helps you activate switches while you are at a different part of the level, for example. Later you can also switch to the clone or create multiple clones (or "past yous", if you will, but calling them clones is easier).

The difficulty of the game comes from avoiding a paradox. Your clones have to end up on the same field and "state" (like pushing a box for example) when they are done mimicking you, otherwise the goal becomes inactive. This can happen when a previously accessible platform is suddenly inaccessible or you stole a box they would have pushed, for example. It is a really cool idea and the first few levels are fun.

The problem with the game is twofold. A lot of levels have a vertical aspect to it where you have to jump down, but thanks to the isometric perspective, a landmass next to another landmass could also be above or below it - it is almost impossible to see what is vertical or not, leading to some trial and error. That trial and error is further exacerbated by the inherent complexity of some of the later levels. Once levels start having multiple clones that have to take multiple routes and interact with each other, it becomes impossible to plan ahead, so you essentially have to try out dozens of routes and interactions until you find the one that works, which was very frustrating and unsatisfying. 

The minimalistic style, while pretty, doesn't help this case either, and it quickly becomes hard to keep an overview. The game then becomes difficult not because of the puzzles, but because it's so hard to keep track of everything you need to do. This lack of visibility is the biggest problem of the game. Switches and platforms also don't show you what gets activated until you press them, which is a pain in bigger levels.

If the verticality and "complexity" was toned down a bit and the focus would lie more on navigation than interaction between different clones, boxes and switches, the game would be a lot more satisfying to play while still retaining the inherent difficulty of dealing with time travel. As it stands, though, some of the later levels require a lot of trial & error to figure out exactly what it is you have to do, and that just isn't fun. Kudos for the idea, but the execution could be a lot better.

[b]TLDR[/b] A very challenging pure puzzle game based on altering time and synchronizing multiple player characters, could use a gentler learning curve. [15/20⭐, 14h🏅, 4/5💡]

[b]Context[/b] Induction is a puzzle game based on time traveling - essentially creating “shadow” versions of the player’s avatar that mirror a previous incarnation. Although not the first game to rely on such mechanics (the best-known probably being one of the worlds of [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/macwh/recommended/26800/]Braid[/url]), Induction is fully built around this concept. 

[b]Writing[/b] It is a pure puzzle game, without any context or plotline.

[b]Aesthetics[/b] The design is elegant and minimalist and accompanied by a suitable, non-intrusive soundtrack. (Although, to be honest, I wasn’t able to figure out what was the rationale behind the level selector.) The fixed isometric perspective is often an obstacle to understanding the level and makes controlling the player character tricky, but as the game progresses you get used to it.

[b]Gameplay[/b]  The puzzles themselves are pretty brutal. I’m all for mind-bending puzzle games, but besides not explaining new concepts or mechanics (which is OK), Induction doesn’t even try to introduce them smoothly with simple levels: they just show up in already complex levels and you’re by yourself to figure them out. (To be honest, I don’t think I’ve ever fully understood all these abilities, and often had to rely on instinct/trial-and-error). Personally, I feel this kind of puzzle games work better when the main challenge is figuring out how to exploit a certain characteristic of the mechanics in a particular level, but then having the actual execution be mostly straightforward ([url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/macwh/recommended/497780/]Recursed[/url] comes to mind, which has similar reality-altering mechanics, but levels were kept to a manageable size). While this happens in Induction midgame, by later stages even after you now what to do you still have to plan long and timed actions, where you spend most time synchronizing events. This ends up being frustrating and undermining the satisfaction of finally solving a level. As any sokoban-like game, there are dead ends but you can always undo by time traveling. The game autosaves but the state of each level is not saved.

[b]Value[/b] It took me 14h to complete the game, for a low price tag. All levels can be revisited from the menu. There is a single progress slot. Achievements are only related to solving the levels, so no added value there. There aren’t used-designed levels, so replay value is tied to revisiting the same levels.

The central idea of this game is pretty cool - you have the ability to reset the level except for your current position, and then a copy of you does all the same movements you did. Using this you can get the copy to activate things that you need to be somewhere else to make use of. A lot of the levels require you to move in such a way that when the copy makes the same movements the effects or context will be different, like crossing a bridge that you can destroy or performing movements after you've moved the copy to a different location.

The main problem I have with this game is the emphasis on timing. Almost all of the puzzles require you to move in a very precise way so that when your copy makes the same movements it will be in the right position for the right amount of time, and I just don't find it fun to deal with a theoretical object at that level of precision. Furthermore the emphasis on timing means that you spend a lot of time in puzzles just sitting around to make sure your copy will give you enough time later, this breaks the cardinal rule of puzzle games in that once you figure out the solution the actual ceremony of solving the puzzle should be fast.

There's another issue on top of the timing and that's the visuals. With the isometric viewpoint it can be very hard to tell where objects and platforms are in relation to each other, and that will definitely cause you to mess up and wreck your puzzle solution from time to time.

If you like the idea of a puzzle game built around time mechanics I recommend Braid. In fact one of the worlds in Braid has pretty much the exact same central copy gimmick as this game.

The idea behind this puzzle game is intriguing. It had the potential to be interesting, too. But… The shortcomings get in the way of playability, solvability, and hence enjoyability.

First up, the controls. Use of standard arrow controls is somewhat expected, except that the game is rotated 45°, so they are endlessly counter-intuitive; one needs effectively to tilt one's head to stay logically aligned with the expected behaviour of the controlled piece.

Then, there's the issue of the minimalistic flatness of design, which makes knowing what one is aligned with - whether one is in the right place for the envisaged move - a matter of guesswork, at best. Combined with the counter-intuitive controls, that makes for endless frustrating mistakes. Along with the lack of perspective, It also makes it impossible to identify whether elements are horizontally or vertically separated (which I suppose it intended).

Thirdly, the rules of the time-looping are not explained. The lack of clarity as to how the different aspects behave - why they behave those ways, why a move that seems perfectly reasonable blocks completion - are a matter of bungled trial and error. (There is iconography used, but it is not informative; certainly not intuitive.)
